newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: U.S. opposes North-South split in UN health agency.
newsitem.headline: U.S. opposes North-South split in UN health agency.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of Health Donna Shalala said on Tuesday she was opposed to allowing the contest for the leadership of the World Health Organisation (WHO) become a North-South battle.

She also told a news conference the world-wide battle against smoking should be a top priority for the new WHO director-general who will take over in July next year when the current incumbent, Hiroshi Nakajima of Japan, steps down.

"I have no intention of us getting pulled into a North-South discussion," she said when asked whether she agreed with a Pakistani statement arguing it was time for a woman from a developing country to get the job.

"The diseases themselves don't know whether they're in a developing country or in a major industrialised country. And I think the leaders of those countries should make decisions on the basis of qualifications."
Pakistan on Monday proposed its own candidate, Nafis Sadik, who has headed the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) for the past decade and is a former hospital doctor and obstetrician by training.
Shalala, who has played a key role in the present U.S. administration's effort to reform the country's welfare system, indicated she thought the 67-year-old Sadik was a strong contender for the post.

The UNFPA chief would be "an enormously attractive candidate (even) if she came from a major industrialised country," she said. But the United States was at present backing no candidate in what was already a strong field.

Another declared candidate for the post, which will be decided next January but is a hot topic at the WHO's current annual Assembly in Geneva, is former Norwegian prime minister Bro Harland Brundtland.

Bolivia on Tuesday announced it was proposing a Nakajima deputy, Fernando Antezana Aranibar, who apart from his medical qualifications is also a graduate of the Kennedy School of Government at Harvard University in the United States.

Shalala, a strong campaigner against the use of tobacco on the U.S. domestic scene, told the news conference smoking "is going to be a growing issue for all of us....as we increasingly see children getting involved with tobacco.

"We are not going to be able to walk away from the tobacco issue, particularly in relationship to our children, because it is one of the fundamental causes of death in the world and imposes a huge cost on every nation on earth," she said.
The WHO would have to tackle the problem head-on, she said.
